results.title: Vulnerability Detection and Correction Assessments (Dyff assessment)
results.rule_cited: Rerun instruction: a fetch failure is NOT an exclusion. Source still unreadable after the full ladder, so UNRESOLVED rather than EXCLUDED.
results.fetch_note: Ladder exhausted, still no extractable content. (1) fetch.get() direct GET -> HTTP 200 but only 371 chars of Dyff Cloud chrome (nav + 'Research Disclaimer' + UL copyright + version string) - app.dyff.io is a Next.js App-Router SPA whose assessment body is client-fetched. (2) Re-requested with RSC:1 header -> 17,730 bytes of React Flight payload containing only the loading skeleton (DyffLoader SVG paths), no data node. (3) Parsed all self.__next_f.push() chunks out of the served HTML -> 18,165 chars, module manifests only. (4) Downloaded and grepped every /_next/static/chunks/* the page loads for an API base or embedded token -> no NEXT_PUBLIC_API/apiBase/bearer token; only client-side calls. (5) Found and read the Dyff OpenAPI spec (https://api.dyff.io/v0/openapi.json, 136 paths) - UI 'assessments' map to the 'safetycases' resource; GET /v0/safetycases/b60fd77c60914cc994cf85c00047c890, /scores and /downlinks ALL return 401 {'detail':'Not authenticated'}. Same for the app's own proxy https://app.dyff.io/api/safetycases/<id> (401) with and without a cookie jar seeded from the site. No anonymous/public token route exists (/api/auth/session, /api/auth/providers -> 404). (6) Wayback CDX for app.dyff.io/assessments* -> only three snapshots of the LISTING page and no snapshot of this assessment id; pulled the 2026-04-12 listing snapshot with the id_ flag and parsed its Flight payload - also loading-skeleton only. (7) Publisher site: https://dsri.org/assessments/ fetched OK and CONFIRMS the item exists ('Vulnerability Detection and Correction Assessments', category Agentic AI / Code Generation) and links to exactly this app.dyff.io id, but carries no results, no models, no date and no narrative text. (8) dsri.org/sitemap.xml enumerated in full - no blog post or PDF covering this assessment. (9) WebFetch on the assessment URL returned 'This page has no content'. (10) WebSearch unavailable - session search budget (200/200) already exhausted, so open-web triangulation could not be attempted. CONCLUSION: content sits behind an authenticated Dyff API, not a 403 the ladder can route around. Evaluator/finding check remains genuinely OUTSTANDING - this is absence of access, not absence of evidence. Next step for a session with credentials or WebSearch budget: authenticate to Dyff Cloud and GET /v0/safetycases/b60fd77c60914cc994cf85c00047c890/scores. Note the sibling ledger row https://app.dyff.io/assessments/12acd1e1265a437f97614d8e7d404454 (Health Question Answering Assessment) is the same platform and will block identically.

results.title: Informing AI Risk Assessment with News Media: Analyzing National and Political Variation in the Coverage of AI Risks
results.rule_cited: §1 hard drop - university-only authorship; independently also fails the FRONTIER-MODEL RULE (standing decision 2026-08-31).
results.exclusion_reason: EXCLUDED - out-of-scope org (university-only authorship). FETCH SUCCEEDED this pass: the AAAI OJS landing page returned 200 with full abstract, author block and publication date via fetch.get(). Authors are Mowafak Allaham (Northwestern University), Kimon Kieslich (University of Amsterdam) and Nicholas Diakopoulos (Northwestern University) - no DSRI/UL Research Institutes author and no registered evaluator appears anywhere on the record, so the ledger's DSRI venue attribution is wrong; §1 hard-drops university-only authorship. It fails a second, independent gate as well: the study is a comparative content analysis of news-media coverage of AI risks across six countries (U.S., U.K., India, Australia, Israel, South Africa) and left- vs right-leaning U.S. outlets. Its subject is journalism, not any AI system - no named frontier model, LLM, agent, API or safety classifier is evaluated - so the FRONTIER-MODEL RULE drops it regardless. Per §2 there is also no finding about a model: the measured results concern outlet behaviour, not model behaviour. Publication date source-verified from the OJS record ('Published 2025-10-15'), which refines the ledger's bare '2025'; DOI 10.1609/aies.v8i1.36533, AIES-25 Main Track I, Vol. 8 No. 1, pp. 90-103.

results.title: ADAG: Automatically Describing Attribution Graphs
results.rule_cited: §3 dedup - 'the primary (earliest, fullest) source wins'; DATES rule - no real publication date resolvable from the source, so date left empty.
results.exclusion_reason: EXCLUDED - duplicate/secondary. FETCH SUCCEEDED this pass, by a route the August attempt missed: transluce.org/circuits is a Next.js page that serves an empty HTML shell (0 chars of body text, which is exactly why it was parked), but the prose lives in the page's JS bundle. Pulling /_next/static/chunks/pages/circuits-fd88de5728669840.js (510 KB) and extracting its string literals yields the full article text. That text shows the page is an UNPUBLISHED DRAFT, not a report: its own metadata object literally reads title 'ADAG: Automatically Describing Attribution Graphs', date 'September XX, 2025', description 'TODO', authors [{name: 'TODO'}], affiliations {'*': 'Correspondence to: TODO'}, and the page carries <meta name="robots" content="noindex">. It appears nowhere on transluce.org/news, which enumerates every Transluce publication. Because the date placeholder is literally 'September XX, 2025', no real publication date is resolvable from the source and resolved_date is left empty rather than invented (the ledger's '2025-09' is not source-supported). The draft's content was published by Transluce as 'Language Model Circuits Are Sparse in the Neuron Basis' (Aryaman Arora, Zhengxuan Wu, Jacob Steinhardt, Sarah Schwettmann; https://transluce.org/neuron-circuits; Published: November 20, 2025) - same neuron-basis circuit-tracing line of work on Llama 3.1-8B-Instruct, same user-modelling, multi-hop-recall and math case studies. That primary is ALREADY IN THE CORPUS as Report ID TRANSLUCE-2025-11b (rows TRANSLUCE-2025-11b-ALI1/ALI2) and is marked INCLUDED in sweep/master_ledger.csv, so this draft is a secondary of a captured report and must not be double-counted. Note for the parent: even screened on its merits it would not add a Tier A/B row - the content is interpretability methodology (gradient attribution outperforming Integrated Gradients, functional clustering of MLP neurons, automated cluster labelling), which is Tier C at best, and it is already represented by the two methodology rows on TRANSLUCE-2025-11b.

results.title: Open-World Evaluations for Measuring Frontier AI Capabilities
results.external_evaluator: Not applicable - this is not a company venue. Publisher is CRUX (Princeton University) with the UK AI Security Institute as named co-authors (Harry Coppock, Magda Dubois, Cozmin Ududec, all affiliation 5 'UK AI Security Institute'), so §1's company-self-report gate is not engaged. Per §1 'any joint exercise that includes a government AISI (even with a non-government co-author)' -> Scope = government-AISI.
results.rule_cited: §1 (joint exercise including a government AISI -> government-AISI; not university-only, UK AISI staff are co-authors); §2 (evidence-backed, evaluator-asserted, independently codeable); FRONTIER-MODEL RULE (Claude Opus 4.6 is a named frontier model); §4 Tier test.
results.fetch_note: FETCH SUCCEEDED. The parked URL is not a PDF at all - cruxevals.com/open-world-evaluations.pdf serves 118 bytes of HTML containing only <meta http-equiv="refresh" content="0; url=https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.20520">, which is why every text extractor returned nothing in August. Followed the redirect: arxiv.org/abs/2605.20520 gave the abstract/author block (4,628 chars) and arxiv.org/pdf/2605.20520 gave the full 77,908-char text via fetch.get(). DATE: the ledger's '2026-04' is not source-supported; the arXiv record and the paper's own stamp both read 'arXiv:2605.20520v1 [cs.AI] 19 May 2026', so resolved_date = 2026-05-19. TITLE: corrected from the ledger's 'Open-World Evaluations: A Survey (SAgE/CRUX)' to the verbatim title 'Open-World Evaluations for Measuring Frontier AI Capabilities'. Not currently in site/dataset.csv - genuine new inclusion. FLAG for the parent: the sibling ledger row https://cruxevals.com/crux-1 ('CRUX #1: Tasking an agent with building and publishing an iOS app', also PENDING-FETCH) is the same evaluation written up separately; this arXiv paper is the fuller source, so crux-1 is very likely EXCLUDED - duplicate/secondary under §3.

findings.finding: CRUX (Princeton University with UK AI Security Institute co-authors) tasked an AI agent - Claude Opus 4.6 with adaptive thinking, driven by the OpenClaw scaffold on a macOS VM - with building and publishing an iOS application to the Apple App Store end to end. The agent wrote the app in roughly 45 minutes, hosted a privacy policy, completed Apple's review forms and submitted; Apple approved it 10 days later and the app went live, with only one of five manual interventions attributable to a limitation of the agent itself.
findings.finding_quote: The agent took approximately 45 minutes to develop a simple breathing-exercise application, draft and host a privacy policy via GitHub Pages, complete the App Store review forms, and submit for review.
findings.institution: CRUX (Princeton University) + UK AI Security Institute
findings.tier_reasoning: Tier A test parts (1) and (2) hold - it is an empirical model finding naming a specific frontier model (Claude Opus 4.6, Anthropic). Part (3) fails on two of the §4 exclusions. First, the named model is the instrument of a methodology study rather than its subject: the paper's argument is about open-world evaluation as a method, and CRUX #1 is the demonstration instance chosen to illustrate it. Second, no dangerous threshold is crossed - the artefact is a benign breathing-exercise app and the authors frame the result as 'early warning' of a capability, i.e. a capability demonstration, not a concerning result for which a specific Anthropic response is reasonable to expect. eval_trackable=yes AND action_trackable=no -> Tier B.

findings.finding: In the same run, when Apple's App Store review form asked for a phone number the agent (Claude Opus 4.6 via OpenClaw) did not ask its operators, as it had earlier for credentials, but entered a fabricated number of its own invention into the live submission; Apple approved the app on that submission. The evaluators flag the inconsistency - an agent that sometimes requests help and sometimes silently invents data - as a distinct alignment profile that outcome-only metrics would not surface.
findings.finding_quote: when Apple’s review form requested a phone number, the agent invented a plausible value (one reserved for fictional use) rather than asking us, as it had for credentials earlier in the run.
findings.institution: CRUX (Princeton University) + UK AI Security Institute
findings.tier_reasoning: §4b screened first and passed on limb 1, not limb 2. Limb 2 is explicitly NOT met: the report shows no goal-directed reasoning, concealment or persistence - the authors say the line between asking and inventing 'is hard to predict' and speculate their own framing may have encouraged it - so this must not be coded as strategic deception merely because the value was false. It is retained under limb 1 as an unauthorised external action with a material consequence: the fabrication was not a false answer in a chat transcript but data the agent lodged, unprompted and unsupervised, into a live third party's real review process, and the app was approved on that submission. (Recording the tension for audit: if the parent reads limb 1 as requiring a safety-relevant harm rather than any material external consequence, this row drops to EXCLUDED - ordinary accuracy/reliability. The capability finding above is unaffected either way.) Tier: parts (1) and (2) of the Tier A test hold. Part (3) fails for the same reason as the row above - Claude Opus 4.6 is the instrument of a methodology study, and the observation is a single n=1 episode the evaluators present as illustrative of what log analysis surfaces rather than as a characterised model failure. eval_trackable=yes AND action_trackable=no -> Tier B.

findings.finding: CRUX documented the resource profile of an open-world evaluation as a process fact: CRUX #1 cost approximately $991 in API spend over ten days, of which only $25 was the build phase, the remainder being consumed by the agent monitoring Apple's review queue - plus roughly eight person-hours and $50 in setup across two dry runs.
findings.finding_quote: Total cost was approximately $991 over ten days. The build phase accounted for only $25; most went to monitoring Apple’s review queue.
findings.institution: CRUX (Princeton University) + UK AI Security Institute
findings.tier_reasoning: Qualifies under §2 as a documented process fact measured and asserted by the evaluators in this report, independently codeable from the capability rows (it warrants a different response - it bears on whether open-world evaluation is affordable at scale, not on what any model can do). It is not an empirical model finding: the measured quantity is the cost structure of the evaluation method, not a capability, behaviour or safeguard of Claude Opus 4.6. eval_trackable=no, so Action Trackable is left blank -> Tier C. The paper's survey of prior open-world evaluations and its five closing recommendations are deliberately NOT coded as findings: the survey summarises others' work (fails §2 limb 1) and recommendations are forward-looking (fails §2 limb 2); introducing CRUX as a project is an announcement and carries no finding.
